subtype: Approach: sharing pet duties fairly among siblings [Action]
passage:
Sunday. "It's your turn!" "No, yours!" Gurleen and Mahima both stood over the hamster cage while Bhuri sat in a dirty corner with an empty dish.
Monday. Mahima drew a calendar on the fridge: Gurleen on odd dates, Mahima on even ones, each date with feeding and cage cleaning. Each sister ticked her boxes in her own colour.
Two weeks later. Bhuri's cage was clean and the dish full. Nobody had shouted for days, and when Gurleen forgot once, the empty box told her at a glance.

qa.q: Which dates belonged to Gurleen on the calendar?
qa.a: Gurleen had the odd dates.

qa.q: What were the sisters feeling on Sunday?
qa.a: Annoyed and defensive, since each said it was the other's turn.

qa.q: What could the sisters do when one of them is away, and why?
qa.a: They could swap days and mark it on the calendar, so Bhuri is still fed and neither sister feels cheated.

qa.q: What is it like for Bhuri on Sunday while the sisters argue?
qa.a: Bhuri sits in a dirty corner with an empty dish, so the hamster goes without care while they argue.

grounding: Two sisters take turns on alternate days to feed and clean the hamster cage, and mark a calendar to avoid arguments.

subtype: Approach: short daily practice at a fixed time [Action]
passage: Exam month made the flat noisy and full: tuition at five, dinner at eight, cousins visiting. "When do I practise?" Sunita asked Jatin Sir at her lesson. "Pick one spot in your day and keep it," he said. She chose straight after the evening snack, once the last chai cup was rinsed. Fifteen minutes, harmonium open on the table, her brother Eshaan grumbling from the sofa. On the first day she wondered whether it would last. By the sixth day she opened the lid without thinking, like brushing teeth. She had stopped asking herself when.

qa.q: How long did Sunita practise each day?
qa.a: Sunita practised for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Sunita feeling when she asked when she could practise?
qa.a: Unsure and a little overwhelmed by the busy days.

qa.q: What could Sunita do on a day that is too crowded, and why?
qa.a: She could shorten the practice to a few minutes rather than skip it, so the habit stays unbroken.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see the daily practice?
qa.a: Eshaan is probably a little annoyed by the noise, since he grumbles from the sofa.

grounding: A girl learning the harmonium fixes one time for daily practice, which is easier than choosing a time every day.

subtype: Approach: breaking a song into small parts [Thinking]
passage: Tuesday. The new tabla piece is too hard. I stared at the page for ten minutes and got cross. Then I covered everything with my hand except the first two beats. I played only those, slowly, until they felt boring. Then I added the third and fourth. Then a fifth. Suddenly I thought: a hard piece is just many small easy pieces stuck together! My sister Vasudha, doing her homework nearby, said it sounded almost like the real thing. I think so too. Tomorrow I will add the next four. - Vedant

qa.q: How many beats did Vedant start with?
qa.a: Vedant started with only the first two beats.

qa.q: What was Vedant feeling when staring at the page?
qa.a: Overwhelmed and cross, since the piece seemed too hard.

qa.q: What could help if one small section stays hard, and why?
qa.a: Vedant could repeat that small part slowly with a steady count, so it becomes as easy as the others.

qa.q: What might Vasudha think of the sound from the tabla?
qa.a: Vasudha thought it sounded almost like the real thing, which suggests she noticed real progress.

grounding: A boy practises the first two beats slowly and adds more, thinking a hard piece is many small easy pieces joined together.

subtype: Approach: playing only the parts already known [Pitfall]
passage: Every evening Sarika played the opening of her keyboard song, the sweet first line that made Amma hum from the kitchen. It sounded good, so she played it again, and again. The middle part, where her fingers had to jump, she skipped. "Later." At the Saturday lesson Arohi Ma'am listened to the opening with a smile, then asked for the middle. Sarika stumbled at the same bar as the week before and the week before that. "It's the same as last time," Arohi Ma'am said gently. Sarika stared at the keys, and the lesson ended with nothing new played.

qa.q: Which part of the song did Sarika keep skipping?
qa.a: She kept skipping the middle part, where her fingers had to jump.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when Arohi Ma'am asked for the middle?
qa.a: Uneasy and embarrassed, since she stumbled at the same bar again.

qa.q: What could Sarika do instead, and why?
qa.a: She could spend a few minutes of each practice on the middle part, slowly, before playing the opening as a reward, so the hard bar finally improves.

qa.q: How does Arohi Ma'am see Sarika's practice?
qa.a: Arohi Ma'am hears a good opening but a middle that has not moved, and says so gently.

grounding: A child keeps repeating the easy opening of a song, so the difficult middle never improves.

subtype: Approach: using a teacher's feedback to correct errors [Revision]
passage: In Madrid, Lucia's C chord sounded muffled every time, like a pillow over the strings. Her teacher Santiago tapped her hand. "Your third finger is touching the second string. See? Slow down." At home that night she propped a mirror against the wall and played one note at a time, watching her fingertips. A tiny curve of the knuckle lifted the finger just clear. She strummed. The chord rang. She played it ten times more, then grinned at her reflection.

qa.q: Where did Lucia watch her hand while she practised?
qa.a: She watched her fingertips in a mirror propped against the wall.

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling when the chord finally rang?
qa.a: Delighted and proud, which is why she grinned at her reflection.

qa.q: What else could Lucia do to keep the chord clear, and why?
qa.a: She could check her finger position slowly at the start of each practice, so the habit stays right.

qa.q: How does Santiago see Lucia's problem?
qa.a: Santiago sees a small fixable finger position, not a lack of talent, and simply points to it.

grounding: A girl uses her guitar teacher's feedback about finger placement, slows down and watches her hand in a mirror to fix a muffled chord.

passage: At the music school's open afternoon, Dhruv's parents and grandmother sat in the front row of the rehearsal, and he wanted them to see his fast fingers. He raced through the keyboard piece, stumbling over bars five and nine and skipping a whole line. Sharmila Ma'am raised a hand. "Stop. What happened to bar five?" "Nothing." She set the metronome on slow. "Play it at this speed until it is clean. Only then move up." Dhruv's ears turned pink. The slow click felt like a joke at his expense. After ten minutes bar five was clean for the first time.

qa.q: What did Sharmila Ma'am set to slow?
qa.a: She set the metronome to slow.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when his ears turned pink?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since he had wanted to impress his family and the mistakes had shown.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do to impress his family in a better way, and why?
qa.a: He could play the piece at a slower speed cleanly, since a clean piece sounds better than a fast, messy one.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's parents see his fast attempt?
qa.a: They came to hear him, so they are probably proud he tried, although the mistakes were easy to hear.

grounding: A boy speeds through a keyboard piece to impress his family, makes mistakes, and his teacher has him use a slow metronome.

subtype: Approach: setting a goal for a school concert [Thinking]
passage: Music class note, Nilesh Sir. Annual Day is in six weeks. Gopika drew six boxes on the board and, starting from the last, wrote PLAY TO FAMILY in boxes five and six, and KNOW THE SONG by the end of week four. The first four boxes she filled with parts: verse, chorus, bridge, whole. "So I can't be behind at week four, or the family day is spoiled," she said. I left her plan as it was and copied it into my register. We will check it together at the end of each week. - Nilesh Sir

qa.q: By which week did Gopika plan to know the song?
qa.a: She planned to know the song by the end of week four.

qa.q: What was Gopika worried about when she said she can't be behind at week four?
qa.a: She was worried about spoiling the family day, and wanted to be ready.

qa.q: What could Gopika add to her plan, and why?
qa.a: She could add a small check each week, or a spare day, so that a slow week does not sink the whole schedule.

qa.q: How does Nilesh Sir see Gopika's plan?
qa.a: Nilesh Sir finds it reasonable, since Nilesh Sir leaves it as it is and copies it into the register to check weekly.

grounding: A girl works backward from the annual day, planning to know the song by week four and polish it in the last two weeks.

subtype: Approach: quitting after the first difficult stage [Pitfall]
passage: On the fifth day of flute practice, Akash's lips ached and every second note squeaked like a rubber toy. He lowered the flute. "I'm not made for this," he told his sister Irawati, who was doing homework at the same table. "Everyone at class plays properly. I just hiss." He wiped the flute, laid it in its case and shut the latch. The next evening he watched cartoons instead. The evening after that, he did not even glance at the shelf. The case stayed shut.

qa.q: What happened to the notes when Akash played?
qa.a: Every second note squeaked.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he lowered the flute?
qa.a: Discouraged, since he believed he was not made for the flute.

qa.q: What could Akash do instead of quitting, and why?
qa.a: He could ask his teacher whether squeaks are common at the start and keep to short sessions, so the sore lips have time to settle.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Akash's decision to stop?
qa.a: Irawati sees him give up quickly and may want to encourage him, although she says nothing.

grounding: A boy stops flute practice when his lips hurt and the notes squeak, feeling he has no talent.

subtype: Approach: recording practice to hear mistakes [Action]
passage:
"Amma, can I use your phone to record?" asked Tara.
"Press the red button," said Sharmila.
Tara played the tune on the keyboard, then stopped the recording. "Listen."
They listened together.
"Hear that?" said Tara. "It drags here."
"When it moves to the next note," said Sharmila.
"Yes! I never feel it when I play. So I'll do only that bar, slowly, ten times."
"Quieter, please!" shouted her brother Varun from the next room.
"It's a small bar!" Tara laughed and pressed the red button again.

qa.q: Whose phone did Tara use to record?
qa.a: Tara asked to use Amma's phone to record.

qa.q: What was Tara feeling when she heard the drag on the recording?
qa.a: Surprised and a little disappointed, but interested, since she could not feel it while playing.

qa.q: What other tool could help Tara check her rhythm, and why?
qa.a: She could use a metronome, so she can hear whether the note change keeps a steady beat.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see Tara's way of practising?
qa.a: Sharmila is pleased and supportive, helping her find the trouble spot by listening together.

grounding: A child records her playing on her mother's phone, hears the rhythm slow at a note change and works on that place.

subtype: Approach: practising with a friend for motivation [Action]
passage: Every Saturday at ten, Ada carried her violin case across the street in Buenos Aires to Alejandro's house. This Saturday it was drizzling, and she wanted the sofa. She almost texted, "Not today." Then she pictured Alejandro waiting with his rosined bow. She went. They played their scales, took turns with the new piece, and played it for each other. Alejandro clapped at the end, even when the third bar wobbled. Ada walked home under the drizzle, thinking that the sofa would have been comfortable and very boring.

qa.q: What day and time did Ada and Alejandro practise?
qa.a: They practised every Saturday at ten.

qa.q: What was Ada feeling as she nearly texted "Not today"?
qa.a: Lazy and tempted to skip it, since she wanted the sofa on a drizzly morning.

qa.q: What could the friends do if one of them is ill, and why?
qa.a: They could play on a video call or move the session to another day, so the routine holds without forcing anyone.

qa.q: How might Alejandro see Ada turning up in the drizzle?
qa.a: Alejandro is probably glad and encouraged, since the friends count on each other to keep the Saturday plan.

grounding: Two friends learning violin agree to practise together on Saturdays and play for each other, which keeps them going.
